client: I've been feeling really on edge lately, and I think it has to do with my partner moving in with me last month. It's like I constantly feel this low-level anxiety, this worry that I'm losing parts of myself and my space that I really need. I'm not even sure talking about it will change anything practical, since we already made this decision together and there's no going back now.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a quiet but persistent unease — not a crisis, but this constant hum of worry that something important to you is slipping away, which is really worth paying attention to. You're right that the practical decision is made, but what we *can* work with is how you're thinking and feeling about it, because that has a huge impact on your day-to-day experience and even the relationship itself. I'm curious — when you notice that feeling of "losing yourself," what specific thoughts or moments tend to trigger it most?

client: Honestly, the moments that hit hardest are when I'm sitting in our apartment and I realize I've just... gone along with whatever he wanted to do that evening, again. Like I'll catch myself thinking "when did I stop having opinions about how I spend my own time?" and it kind of startles me. It's not that he's forcing anything, it's more like I've just gradually faded into the background of my own life.
therapist: That image of "fading into the background of your own life" is really striking, and it makes sense that catching yourself in those moments would feel unsettling — like a quiet alarm going off. What's worth exploring here is whether this pattern of going along is something new that living together has created, or whether it might be a tendency you've had before that this new closeness is just making more visible. When you think back, do you notice yourself doing this in other areas of your life too, or does it feel specific to your relationship with him?

client: Honestly, when I think about it... yeah, it's not just with him. I do it at work too — I'll have an opinion in a meeting and just stay quiet because it feels easier than dealing with the pushback. But I think it feels sharper with him because he's supposed to be the person I'm closest to, so when I disappear even there, it feels more... I don't know, more like a verdict on who I am.
therapist: That last part you said is really important — that it feels like "a verdict on who I am," as if disappearing in your closest relationship is somehow proof of something being fundamentally wrong with you, rather than a habit you've learned that's been working as a kind of self-protection. In CBT terms, we'd want to gently challenge that leap — the behavior of going quiet is something you *do*, not something you *are*, and it sounds like it developed for understandable reasons. What do you think you're most afraid would happen if you did voice your opinion — whether in that meeting or with your partner at home?

client: I hear what you're saying about it being something I *do* versus something I *am*, and I want to believe that, I really do. But honestly, when I imagine actually speaking up, what comes up immediately is this fear that people will just... look at me like I've said something stupid, or that my partner will get frustrated and pull away even more. It's like the risk of being dismissed or losing connection feels so much worse than just staying quiet and at least keeping the peace.
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense — you've essentially built a calculation where silence feels like the safer bet, because the cost of being dismissed or losing closeness feels unbearable compared to the cost of just going along. But it's worth gently noticing that staying quiet has its own hidden cost, which is exactly what you've been describing — that slow fading, that loss of yourself — so neither option feels safe right now. When you imagine your partner actually responding with frustration or dismissal after you spoke up, how likely do you think that really is — and is there any evidence from your relationship that might challenge or support that fear?

client: Honestly, when I really think about it... there have been times when I brought something up and they didn't completely shut me down. Like, there was that one conversation about my work stress where they actually listened for a while. But my mind keeps jumping straight to the times it went badly, and those moments feel so much louder than the good ones, so it's hard to trust that the good ones are actually the pattern.
therapist: What you just did there is actually really significant — you went looking for evidence and you *found* it, even though your mind didn't offer it up easily. What you're describing has a name in CBT: it's called a negativity bias, where threatening or painful experiences get stored more vividly and feel more "true" than the quieter, safer ones, even when the safer ones are just as real. That conversation about your work stress where they actually listened — that's data too, and it deserves just as much weight as the harder moments. What do you think it would feel like to deliberately hold onto that example the next time you're on the edge of going quiet with him?

client: I hear what you're saying about the negativity bias, and honestly it makes sense when you explain it like that. But I'm not sure I'd actually remember that conversation in the moment — when I start to feel like he's going to dismiss me, it's like a switch flips and all I can think about is protecting myself. It feels almost too fast to catch, like by the time I'd remember the good example, I'd already be halfway into my shell.
therapist: What you're describing — that lightning-fast switch into self-protection — is actually one of the most important things we could work with, because you're right that in-the-moment reasoning is really hard when that alarm is already firing. One approach in CBT is to do the work *before* the moment arrives, almost like a fire drill — so that a grounding thought or reminder becomes almost automatic, rather than something you have to consciously retrieve under pressure. If you were going to choose one small, simple phrase or image to anchor yourself to — something that captures "I have evidence I can be heard" — what might feel true enough to actually stick?

client: I hear what you're saying about the fire drill idea, and part of me gets it, but I'm also sitting here trying to think of a phrase that feels true and... I'm kind of drawing a blank, which is frustrating. Like, the honest thing in my head is something like "people have listened before," but even as I say it out loud it feels kind of weak and unconvincing, like I don't fully believe it. I guess I'm worried that if the phrase doesn't feel solid enough in a calm moment, it's definitely not going to hold up when I'm actually panicking.
therapist: The frustration you're feeling right now is actually really valuable information — it's telling us that you're not someone who can just paste a positive affirmation over a deep fear and have it stick, and that's not a flaw, that's honesty. A phrase only becomes convincing through experience, not just repetition, which means the real "fire drill" might be less about finding the perfect words and more about taking small, low-stakes risks with your partner and letting those moments build the evidence your nervous system actually needs to trust. What might be the smallest possible version of speaking up with him — something almost too small to feel scary — that you could try this week just to start collecting that proof for yourself?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me appreciates that you're not just telling me to think positive or whatever. But when you ask about the "smallest possible version," my mind kind of goes blank, because even tiny things with him feel loaded — like if I mention I didn't like how he dismissed something I said last week, I'm already imagining him getting defensive and then me feeling worse than before. I guess I'm scared that even the small attempts will just give me more evidence that it's not safe, not less.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense — it's not irrational to worry that a small attempt could backfire and actually deepen the wound rather than heal it, and I don't want to push you toward something that feels genuinely unsafe. But I'm noticing something worth sitting with: right now, avoiding the risk feels protective, but it also means the only evidence your nervous system ever gets to collect is the absence of connection, which quietly keeps confirming the fear. I'm wondering — is there a version of "speaking up" that isn't about raising something difficult with him at all, but just expressing a small preference, like suggesting what to have for dinner or what to watch, somewhere with almost no emotional stakes attached?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I guess that makes sense logically — like, start small with something that doesn't matter. But even that feels weirdly loaded with my dad, because if I suggest something and he dismisses it or just ignores it, I think that would actually hurt more than saying nothing. It's like even the small stuff has become evidence in some ongoing case I'm building about whether he actually sees me.
therapist: I want to gently pause on something — you just said "my dad" rather than your partner, and I don't think that was a slip worth rushing past, because it sounds like this fear of not being seen might have roots that go much deeper than this relationship or even this apartment. It makes so much sense that even small moments feel like they're part of a bigger verdict, if somewhere along the way you learned that the people closest to you might not really see you. Can you tell me a little about what it was like to try to be heard by your dad growing up?

client: Yeah, I noticed I said that too, and I wasn't sure if I should correct it or just let it go. Growing up, my dad was... present, I guess, but not really there, if that makes sense. Like I could be talking right at him and he'd be looking through me, like I was just background noise in his own life.
therapist: What you just described — being looked through, like background noise — is such a painful way to grow up, and it makes profound sense that this became the template your nervous system learned to expect from the people closest to you. That little boy who kept trying to be seen by his dad didn't disappear; he's still there in the apartment, still keeping score, still waiting to find out if this time it will be different. I'm wondering — when you imagine your partner truly seeing you and taking you seriously, does it feel like something you can picture and believe in, or does it feel almost foreign, like something that happens for other people?
